newsitem.title: USA: FOCUS-COMMODITIES IMPROVING, LED BY OIL, GRAINS.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-COMMODITIES IMPROVING, LED BY OIL, GRAINS.

text.p: The outlook for commodities prices is improving again, looking out into the second half of the year, led by improving supply/demand fundamentals in the energy and in the grains and oilseeds sector, analysts said.

"Part of the previous weakness in commodities as a group was related to the normal negative seasonal patterns, and while the overall bearish summer seasonal influence is not quite over, some markets may be starting to anticipate the more bullish fall seasonal period," Merrill Lynch commodities research director, Bill O'Neill said.
"The rally (of the past month in commodities prices) was broad based and included corn, soybeans, crude oil and products, cattle, and to some extent base and precious metals," he said.

After sliding to an 18 month low at 180.71 points in July, the GSCI (Goldman Sachs Commodity Index), which has a 49 percent weighting in the energy sector, recovered nearly 10 percent to 198.35 this week.

The GSCI's five-day (weekly) moving-average has crossed back above both its 21-day (monthly) average and its 55-day (quarterly) average, suggesting the downtrend from record highs at 231.82 in January this year may be over.

The CRB (Commodities Research Bureau) price index, which has a 47 percent weighting in the agricultural sector, recovered about five percent in the past month to 245.30 points, from a two year low at 232.01 in July.
Similarly, the CRB's five-day average has crossed back above its 21-day and 55-day averages.

"We believe that short term problems are now resolving, and we have consequently raised our overall GSCI returns forecast to 15 percent, and the energy sub-index returns forecast to 18 percent," Goldman Sachs commodities research director, Steve Strongin, said.
The GSCI Returns Index is up 6.38 pct for the quarter to date, though is still down 3.27 pct for the year to date.
The Returns Index is based on investing in commodities as an asset class by means of the CME GSCI futures and rolling the long position forward each month.
ENERGY SECTOR:

After seeing an 18 month low at $18.41 a barrel in June, benchmark nearby NYMEX crude oil futures, which tend to lead IPE Brent futures and the physical crude oil grades, have climbed back above $20.00 a barrel.

"Surprising revisions to the world (oil) supply and demand situation in the most recent IEA (International Energy Agency) forecast reveal a market that appears balanced through the end of the year," said Philip Verleger, Maryland-based editor of "The Petroleum Economics Monthly".
"Under this projection, the recent forecasts for weak oil prices published here in other sources need to be rethought."
In its July forecasts the IEA boosted projections for oil demand by 400,000 barrels per day (bpd) in the second quarter 1997 and by 100,000 bpd for the 1997 year as a whole.

Meanwhile, the IEA also reduced its forecast increase in non-OPEC oil production by 200,000 bpd in the second quarter and by 100,000 bpd for the third quarter, though the forecast for the 1997 year was unchanged.
The effect of these changes was to raise the call-on-OPEC-crude oil by 600,000 bpd in the second quarter and by 200,000 bpd for the year.
But the IEA traditionally underestimates oil demand and overestimates supply, so the supply/demand balance may get tighter, analysts said.
"We originally thought that the oil market would remain in mild surplus through summer and move back into deficit in the fall," Strongin said.
"It now appears that the market moved back into deficit in June and that most of the inventory build that took place in the first half of this year has already been absorbed."

U.S. crude oil stocks fell by 15 million barrels in July and are now four million barrels below year-ago levels, while in Europe crude oil stocks fell by 12 million barrels in June and are now nine million barrels below last year.

But bearish analysts warn of a short term surge in Iraqi oil exports now the second U.N.-Iraq oil-for-food deal has been agreed, and see the strongest El Nino global weather pattern since 1982/83 as likely to produce a mild U.S. and European winter in 1997/98, reducing heating oil requirements.

"Both NYMEX crude and heating oil have a strong seasonal tendency to hit their price peaks late in the third quarter or early in the fourth quarter, before embarking on a period of extended weakness stretching well into the first quarter," Smith Barney analyst John Saucer said.
GRAINS, OILSEEDS SECTOR:
CBOT wheat and corn prices have recovered from two year lows in the past month, while CBOT soybeans have recovered from nine month lows.
"A 1997/98 grain rally seems to have started even earlier than we had expected," Goldman Sach's Strongin said.
"While record or near record U.S. soybean and corn harvests are likely, the real story is the tightness that continues to characterize the global grains system."
"One main reason why the 1997/98 grain market is so likely to be tight is that the global oilseed acreage has increased dramatically this year at the expense of grains," he said.

The change in planting patterns has largely resulted from the greater autonomy farmers now have as a result of the GATT Uruguay Round Agriculture Agreement and the changes to U.S. farm subsidy legislation, analysts said.

"While the current shortage of soybeans is likely to ease with the harvest, much of that relief is due to a large acreage shift away from other crops which is likely to cause a production shortfall in those crops," Strongin said.

The global El Nino weather pattern, a global weather phenomenon triggered by a reversal of normal tradewind and water circulation patterns in the South Pacific, may also cause supply shocks for agricultural markets, analysts said.
The El Nino typically generates wetter and milder winters in North America and Europe, but droughts in the southern hemisphere.

Already in recent weeks, parts of Poland, Germany and Hong Kong have experienced their worst floods in nearly a century, while heavy rains have been seen along the western coasts of the Americas, and the corn belt has seen a dry spell.
The Indian monsoon was late and Indonesia, Thailand and Australia face the potential for drought conditions.

Dryness in central Asia is threatening Chinese crop production and has already destroyed 600,000 tonnes of the Kazak wheat crop which represents about 7.1 percent of local production, though only 0.1 percent of world output.
All of this has occurred before the peak of El Nino's likely impact, which should be between November 1997 and January 1998, analysts noted.

"Weather uncertainty has supported a stronger (soybean) price trend since the early July low of $5.77 per bushel basis the November contract," Merrill Lynch analyst Mario Balleto said. "If severe crop stress develops during August, prices could become explosive, he said."
